newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's high finance council wants deficit down.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's high finance council wants deficit down.

text.p: Belgium's High Finance Council, a government advisory body made up of central bank and treasury officials, said on Tuesday growth would remain modest in 1997 and 1998, but urged the government to continue cutting the budget deficit anyway.

In its annual report, the HFC said it expected Belgian gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by around 2.0 percent, down from a 2.4 percent estimate made a year ago, accelerating to 2.4 percent in 1998.
It also forecast the 1997 public deficit at around 2.8 percent of GDP, down from a revised 3.2 percent in 1996.
The HFC said the government, in cooperation with Belgium's regions, should aim to reduce the public deficit further in 1998 to 2.3 percent of GDP.
"These objectives would permit a durable reduction of the indebtedness of all the public authorities, confirming the trend which the (HFC) outlined in its 1995 report," the HFC said.

Reducing the 1998 net borrowing requirement could be achieved by lifting Belgium's primary surplus (its balance of revenue and spending before debt service costs) to 5.6 percent from a forecast 5.3 percent in 1997.

The HFC said it made its recommendations on the basis of the assumption that inflation would average 1.9 percent in 1997 and 2.0 percent in 1998 and long-term interest rate levels in those years of respectively 5.8 percent and 6.2 percent.

It noted that short term interest rates were expected to start rising again during the course of 1998, which would mean the average interest rate on its debt stabilising at around 6.5 percent -- the same as expected in 1997.
The HFC's recommendations are addressed not only at Belgium's federal government, but also its Dutch, French and German speaking communities, each of which is responsible for certain budgetary areas.
